topic.title: Auth
topic.summary: Sessions, tokens, OAuth, OIDC, SAML, and the authorization models on top of them: how systems know who is calling and what they may do.

cards.title: Authentication vs authorization
cards.body: Authentication answers "who are you," authorization answers "what may you do." They fail differently: an authentication failure is a 401 and means try again with credentials; an authorization failure is a 403 and means credentials were fine, permission was not. Systems mix them up constantly, returning 403 for expired tokens or 401 for forbidden resources. Keep them as separate layers in code: one component establishes identity, a different one decides access. Everything else in auth builds on this split.
cards.seniorNote: If your API can't tell a 401 from a 403, your access control is probably muddled too.

cards.title: Sessions: the classic model
cards.body: On login, the server creates a random session ID, stores the user's identity against it server-side (in memory, Redis, or a database), and sends the ID back in a cookie. Every later request carries the cookie; the server looks up the session and knows who's calling. The state lives on the server, which makes logout and revocation trivial: delete the row. The cost is a lookup on every request, and the store must be shared across all app instances.
cards.seniorNote: Sessions scale fine. "Sessions don't scale" usually means "we didn't want to run Redis."

cards.title: JWT anatomy
cards.body: A JSON Web Token is three base64url segments joined by dots: a header naming the signing algorithm, a payload of claims such as sub (subject), iss (issuer), aud (audience), exp (expiry), and iat (issued at), and a signature over the first two. Anyone can decode it; only the key holder can produce a valid signature. A JWT proves that the issuer said these claims at that time. It is not encrypted by default, so it must never carry secrets.
cards.seniorNote: A JWT is a signed statement, not a secret. Treat the payload as public.

cards.title: Sessions vs JWTs
cards.body: The real difference is where the state lives. Sessions keep it on the server; the cookie is just a pointer. JWTs move it into the token itself; the server verifies a signature and trusts the claims without a lookup. That buys statelessness and cheap horizontal scaling, and costs you revocation: a signed token stays valid until it expires, whatever happened since. Mature systems use both: JWTs for short-lived access, server-side state for the long-lived refresh token.
cards.seniorNote: Stateless tokens trade revocation for scale. Know which one your product can afford to lose.

cards.title: JWT failure modes
cards.body: The classic bugs: accepting alg: none, so an unsigned token passes; letting the token choose its algorithm, so an RSA public key gets used as an HMAC secret; forgetting to check aud, so a token for one service works on another; omitting exp entirely; signing with a weak or shared secret. Every one has caused real breaches. Use a maintained library, pin the expected algorithm, and validate iss, aud, and exp on every request, not just at login.
cards.seniorNote: Never let the token tell you how to verify the token.

cards.title: Opaque tokens and introspection
cards.body: An opaque token is a random string with no internal structure. The resource server can't read it; it calls the authorization server's introspection endpoint to ask "is this valid, and for whom?" That restores instant revocation and keeps claims off the wire, at the cost of a network hop per request, usually softened by short caching. Opaque tokens are common for first-party APIs and refresh tokens; JWTs win when many services must verify without a central call.
cards.seniorNote: Opaque outside, JWT inside is a common pattern: exchange at the gateway, verify locally downstream.

cards.title: OAuth 2.0: the problem it solves
cards.body: OAuth exists so a user can let one application access their data in another without sharing a password. Before it, "import your contacts" meant giving a stranger your email password. OAuth replaces that with delegated, scoped, revocable access tokens. Crucially, OAuth is an authorization framework: it says what a client may do, not who the user is. Using a bare OAuth access token as proof of identity is a well-known mistake that OpenID Connect was created to fix.
cards.seniorNote: OAuth answers "may this app read my calendar," not "who is logged in."

cards.title: The four roles
cards.body: Every OAuth flow involves the same cast. The resource owner is the user who owns the data. The client is the app requesting access. The authorization server authenticates the user, gets consent, and issues tokens. The resource server hosts the protected API and accepts those tokens. Often the authorization and resource servers belong to one company, like Google, but they are logically separate. Keeping the roles straight makes every flow readable: who redirects whom, who holds a secret, who validates.
cards.seniorNote: When a flow diagram confuses you, label the four roles first. The arrows follow.

cards.title: Authorization code flow
cards.body: The default flow for apps with a backend. The client redirects the browser to the authorization server with its client ID, requested scopes, a redirect URI, and a random state value. The user logs in and consents. The server redirects back with a short-lived authorization code. The client's backend exchanges that code, plus its client secret, for an access token over a direct server-to-server call. The browser only ever sees the code, never the token.
cards.seniorNote: The code is single-use and short-lived. The token never touches the front channel.

cards.title: Front channel, back channel
cards.body: The code exchange exists because of the browser. Anything passing through redirects and URLs is the front channel: visible in history, logs, referrer headers, and to extensions. The direct call from backend to authorization server is the back channel: TLS, authenticated by the client secret, invisible to the user's device. OAuth deliberately puts only a worthless-alone code on the front channel and the valuable token on the back channel. Every flow variation is about what happens without a back channel.
cards.seniorNote: If a token appears in a URL, something has gone wrong in the design.

cards.title: PKCE and the death of implicit flow
cards.body: Single-page apps and mobile apps have no server to hold a client secret. The old answer was the implicit flow, returning the token in the URL fragment, which leaked. PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) fixed it: the client generates a random verifier, sends its hash with the initial request, then sends the verifier with the code exchange. An attacker who intercepts the code cannot complete the exchange. PKCE is now recommended for every client, with or without a secret.
cards.seniorNote: If someone proposes implicit flow today, they learned OAuth from an old tutorial.

cards.title: Client credentials: machine to machine
cards.body: When there is no user, use the client credentials flow: the client authenticates directly to the authorization server with its ID and secret and receives an access token scoped to itself. It's the flow for cron jobs, backend services, and CI pipelines calling APIs. No consent screen, no redirect. The risk is entirely in secret management: rotate secrets, store them in a vault, and prefer workload identity (short-lived, platform-issued credentials) over long-lived static secrets wherever the platform supports it.
cards.seniorNote: A static client secret in an env var is a password that never expires.

cards.title: Scopes and consent
cards.body: Scopes are the permission language of OAuth: strings like read:calendar or repo:write that the client requests and the user approves. The access token carries the granted set, and the resource server enforces it. Good scope design is coarse enough to fit on a consent screen and fine enough to follow least privilege. Requesting everything up front is a smell; incremental authorization, asking only when needed, is the mature pattern. Scopes are coarse; per-resource authorization still lives in your app.
cards.seniorNote: Scopes gate the client. They don't replace checking whether this user may see this row.

cards.title: Short access tokens, long refresh tokens
cards.body: Access tokens should live minutes, not days. That bounds the damage of a leak and makes JWT's missing revocation tolerable. To avoid logging users in every fifteen minutes, the authorization server also issues a refresh token: long-lived, stored securely, presented only to the authorization server to mint new access tokens. The refresh token is server-tracked, so it can be revoked. The split gives stateless verification on every API call and stateful control at the point of renewal.
cards.seniorNote: Access token TTL is your revocation latency. Set it like you mean it.

cards.title: Refresh token rotation and reuse detection
cards.body: Because refresh tokens are long-lived, they are the prize an attacker wants. Rotation issues a new refresh token with every use and invalidates the old one. Reuse detection adds the trap: if an already-used refresh token shows up again, someone has a stolen copy, so revoke the entire token family and force re-login. This turns a silent, persistent compromise into a loud, self-terminating one. Most modern authorization servers support it; enable it, especially for public clients.
cards.seniorNote: Rotation alone isn't enough. Reuse detection is what makes theft self-defeating.

cards.title: OIDC: identity on top of OAuth
cards.body: OpenID Connect adds the missing "who" to OAuth 2.0. Same flows, same roles, plus an ID token: a JWT about the user, with claims like sub (a stable user identifier), email, name, and the crucial aud and nonce. The ID token is for the client, to establish a login session. The access token is for the resource server, to call APIs. Treating them as interchangeable is the most common OIDC bug. "Sign in with Google" is OIDC, not bare OAuth.
cards.seniorNote: ID token proves who logged in. Access token proves what may be called. Never swap them.

cards.title: What "Login with Google" actually does
cards.body: The user clicks the button; your app redirects to Google with scope openid and a nonce. Google authenticates them and redirects back with a code. Your backend exchanges it and receives an ID token. You verify the signature against Google's published keys, check iss, aud, exp, and that nonce matches. Only then do you trust sub as the user's identity and create your own session. Your session, not Google's token, is what the user carries afterwards.
cards.seniorNote: The IdP authenticates. Your app still owns the session and the user record.

cards.title: Discovery and JWKS
cards.body: Resource servers verify JWTs without calling the issuer on every request. The issuer publishes a discovery document at a well-known URL listing its endpoints and a JWKS URL: a JSON set of public keys, each with a key ID. A token's header carries the kid; the verifier fetches the matching key, caches it, and checks the signature locally. Key rotation just means publishing a new key alongside the old one. Cache keys, but refresh on an unknown kid.
cards.seniorNote: If your service hardcodes the IdP's public key, the next key rotation is your outage.

cards.title: SAML: the enterprise protocol
cards.body: SAML predates OAuth and still dominates enterprise single sign-on. It exchanges XML assertions, signed statements about a user, between an identity provider (Okta, Microsoft Entra) and a service provider (your app). The browser posts the assertion to your app; you validate the signature and create a session. Same shape as OIDC, older technology: XML signatures are notoriously easy to get wrong, and metadata exchange is manual. When enterprise customers ask for SSO, they mean SAML, at least as an option.
cards.seniorNote: Support SAML because customers demand it, not because you want it. Use a library.

cards.title: SAML vs OIDC
cards.body: Both do federated login. OIDC is JSON, JWT-based, mobile-friendly, and the default for anything built this decade. SAML is XML, browser-redirect-based, and entrenched in enterprise IT. Choose OIDC for consumer login and new integrations; support SAML when selling to companies whose IdP admins expect it. Many products run both behind one abstraction: the app sees a normalised "authenticated user" object, and the protocol is an adapter. That abstraction is the senior design decision; the protocol choice is a checkbox.
cards.seniorNote: Design the identity abstraction first. Protocols plug into it.

cards.title: IdP-initiated vs SP-initiated
cards.body: In SP-initiated login, the user starts at your app, which redirects them to the identity provider and expects a response tied to that request. In IdP-initiated login, the user starts at the company portal, clicks your app's tile, and arrives with an unsolicited assertion. SP-initiated is safer because you can bind the response to a request you made (state, nonce, RelayState). IdP-initiated is harder to protect against replay and injection. Support it if customers insist; prefer the other.
cards.seniorNote: Unsolicited assertions are a login you didn't ask for. Treat them with suspicion.

cards.title: Single logout is a lie
cards.body: Logging out of one app should log you out everywhere, in theory. In practice, single logout requires every service provider to accept and act on a logout notification, front-channel or back-channel, and any one failing leaves a zombie session. Add JWTs that remain valid until expiry and the picture worsens. Realistic strategy: short access tokens, server-side session revocation, revoke the refresh token, and accept that "logged out everywhere" means "within a few minutes."
cards.seniorNote: Promise "logged out within N minutes," not "instantly." Then make N small.

cards.title: Where tokens live in the browser
cards.body: localStorage is readable by any script on the page, so one XSS bug hands an attacker every token. An HttpOnly cookie is invisible to JavaScript, defeating that, but the browser sends it automatically, which enables CSRF. The mature answer: keep tokens in HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies, and defend CSRF separately. For SPAs, a backend-for-frontend pattern lets the server hold tokens and give the browser only a session cookie. A refresh token in localStorage is close to indefensible.
cards.seniorNote: XSS steals what JavaScript can read. Make the important thing unreadable.

cards.title: CSRF and SameSite
cards.body: Cross-site request forgery exploits automatic cookie sending: a malicious page makes your browser submit a request to a site you're logged into. The classic defence is a synchroniser token the attacker's page can't know. SameSite cookies cut most of it off at the browser: Lax blocks cookies on cross-site POSTs, Strict blocks them on all cross-site requests. Modern browsers default to Lax. Still set it explicitly, and keep a token check on state-changing endpoints.
cards.seniorNote: SameSite is your first CSRF layer, not your only one.

cards.title: The resource server's checklist
cards.body: Every request with a bearer token gets the same checks, in order: signature valid against a trusted key; iss matches the expected issuer; aud includes this service; exp is in the future, with a small clock-skew allowance; nbf, if present, has passed; the required scopes are present. Then, and only then, map sub to a local identity and apply application authorization. Skipping aud is the classic mistake: a token minted for one API silently works on another.
cards.seniorNote: Verification is a checklist, not a vibe. Encode it once, in one place.

cards.title: Validate at the edge, trust inside
cards.body: A common architecture: the API gateway validates the external token, then forwards requests to internal services with the caller's identity in a header or an internal token. Internal services trust that header. This works only if the network guarantees the header can't be spoofed, meaning nothing but the gateway can reach those services. The moment an internal service is exposed, or a compromised pod can call another, the trust collapses. Zero-trust architectures re-verify at every hop for exactly that reason.
cards.seniorNote: A trusted header is a security boundary. Make sure the network actually enforces it.

cards.title: Service-to-service identity
cards.body: Services need to prove who they are to each other. Options, roughly from weakest to strongest: shared API keys, client-credentials OAuth tokens, mutual TLS where each service holds a certificate, and workload identity frameworks like SPIFFE that issue short-lived certificates automatically. Service meshes such as Istio provide mTLS transparently. The goal is the same as for user auth: short-lived, automatically rotated, verifiable credentials, with no long-lived secret sitting in a config file.
cards.seniorNote: The question is "how does service A prove it's A?" A static key in config isn't proof.

cards.title: RBAC, ABAC, ReBAC
cards.body: Role-based access control assigns permissions to roles and roles to users: simple, auditable, and it breaks down when you need "editors of this project only." Attribute-based control evaluates rules over attributes of user, resource, and context: flexible, harder to reason about. Relationship-based control (Google's Zanzibar, OpenFGA) models permissions as a graph: user X is editor of doc Y, doc Y is in folder Z. Most products start with RBAC and add relationships when sharing or multi-tenancy arrives.
cards.seniorNote: RBAC answers "what role." ReBAC answers "on which thing." Products with sharing need the second.

cards.title: Where authorization decisions live
cards.body: Scattering if user.role == 'admin' across the codebase guarantees drift. Centralise the decision: a policy layer (Open Policy Agent, Cedar, or a dedicated authorization service) answers "may this subject do this action on this resource," and application code only asks. Enforcement stays local; decision logic becomes one auditable place. The trade-off is latency and a new dependency; mitigate with local evaluation or caching. Authorization changes often, so treat it as data, not as scattered code.
cards.seniorNote: "Who can do what" should be answerable by reading one thing, not grepping the codebase.

cards.title: Multi-tenancy and the tenant claim
cards.body: In a multi-tenant system, the most damaging bug is cross-tenant access: a user from company A reads company B's data via a guessable ID. Defence in depth: put the tenant identifier in the token as a claim, derive it from the token on every request rather than from the URL or body, and scope every database query by it, ideally at the data-access layer so no query can forget. Row-level security in the database is a good backstop.
cards.seniorNote: Never take tenant ID from the request. Take it from the verified identity.

cards.title: Revocation strategies
cards.body: Stateless tokens can't be recalled, so you build around it. Keep access tokens short-lived. Revoke at the refresh token, which is server-tracked. For "log out everywhere" or a compromised account, add a session version: a counter per user, included in the token, and reject tokens whose version is stale; a single cached integer lookup. A denylist of revoked token IDs works for rare emergencies but grows without bound. Pick the cheapest option that meets your revocation latency target.
cards.seniorNote: Session versioning gives you instant global revocation for one cached integer per user.

cards.title: MFA, passkeys, and the password's decline
cards.body: Passwords alone fail against phishing and credential stuffing. Multi-factor adds something you have: TOTP codes, push approval, or hardware keys. SMS codes are the weakest, vulnerable to SIM swapping. Passkeys, built on WebAuthn, replace the password with a device-bound key pair: the site stores a public key, the device signs a challenge, and phishing fails because the credential is bound to the origin. Adoption is accelerating; new consumer products should plan for passkeys as a first-class option.
cards.seniorNote: Phishing-resistant means bound to the origin. TOTP isn't; passkeys are.

cards.title: The confused deputy
cards.body: A confused deputy is a service tricked into using its own authority on an attacker's behalf. In auth, the classic forms: your backend accepts an access token meant for a different app because you skipped the aud check, or forwards a user's token to a third-party API that then acts with your app's privileges. Defences: validate audience, never forward tokens beyond their intended recipient, and use token exchange to mint a narrowly scoped token for downstream calls.
cards.seniorNote: Every token has an intended audience. Using it elsewhere is the bug class.

cards.title: The interview question: design login
cards.body: "Design authentication for our app" is a scoping test. The senior answer starts with questions: consumer or enterprise, first-party only or third-party API access, web, mobile, or both. Then a shape: OIDC with an external IdP or your own authorization server, authorization code with PKCE for every client, short-lived JWT access tokens, rotated refresh tokens with reuse detection, HttpOnly cookies on web, JWKS-based verification at the gateway, a policy layer for authorization. Then the trade-offs you'd revisit.
cards.seniorNote: The answer is a set of decisions with reasons, not a list of technologies.

cards.title: Debugging a burst of 401s or 403s
cards.body: A burst of 401s after a deploy almost always means verification broke: rotated signing keys with a stale cache, a changed issuer URL, clock skew on a new host, or an audience mismatch after a config change. A burst of 403s means identity worked and permission logic changed: a role migration, a policy update, a missing tenant claim. Check token claims first with a decoder, then the verifier's key cache, then policy. Log the failure reason, never the token.
cards.seniorNote: Log why a token was rejected. It turns an hour of guessing into a one-line fix.

cards.title: Auth incidents seniors have seen
cards.body: The recurring incidents: a token in a URL that landed in analytics logs; a refresh token in localStorage stolen by a third-party script; a service that skipped aud and accepted tokens from a sister app; an IdP key rotation that took down every service with a hardcoded key; an admin flag read from the request body; an internal service left reachable without the gateway. None are exotic. Each is a missed line in the checklist from the earlier cards.
cards.seniorNote: Auth incidents are rarely clever. They're checklists that weren't followed.

quiz.prompt: A token issued for your billing API is accepted by your reporting API. Which check was most likely skipped?

options.text: exp
aud
iat
Signature

quiz.explanation: The token was validly signed and unexpired; it just wasn't meant for reporting. Only the audience claim encodes which service a token is for.

quiz.prompt: You're building a mobile app with no backend of its own. Which OAuth flow should it use?

options.text: Implicit flow, since there's no server to hold a secret
Authorization code flow with PKCE
Client credentials flow with the secret embedded in the app
Authorization code flow with a client secret in the app bundle

quiz.explanation: PKCE lets a public client complete the code exchange safely without a secret. Implicit leaks the token in the URL, and any secret shipped in an app bundle is public.

quiz.prompt: After "Login with Google," your frontend calls your API. Which token should it send?

options.text: The Google ID token, since it proves who the user is
An access token or session issued for your API
The authorization code
The refresh token, since it lasts longest

quiz.explanation: The ID token is for the client to establish a login. APIs consume access tokens (or your own session) whose audience is that API. Refresh tokens go only to the authorization server.

quiz.prompt: Your auth server sees a refresh token that was already rotated being presented again. What's the right response?

options.text: Issue a new access token; the old refresh token was valid once
Revoke the entire token family and force re-login
Ignore it silently
Extend the access token TTL to reduce refresh calls

quiz.explanation: A rotated token reappearing means two parties hold it, one of them an attacker. Killing the whole family ends the compromise regardless of who presented it.

quiz.prompt: For a web app, which storage choice best limits the damage of an XSS bug?

options.text: localStorage, because it isn't sent automatically
sessionStorage, because it clears on tab close
HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies plus CSRF defence
A JavaScript variable in memory only

quiz.explanation: XSS can read anything JavaScript can read. HttpOnly cookies are unreadable from script; SameSite and a CSRF token handle the automatic-sending problem that cookies introduce.

quiz.prompt: In a multi-tenant API, where should the tenant ID used to scope database queries come from?

options.text: The URL path, e.g. /tenants/123/orders
A header the client sets
A claim in the verified token
The request body

quiz.explanation: Anything the client sends can be altered to another tenant's ID. Only a claim inside a token the server verified is trustworthy.
